questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] consuming payment webhooks when the provider, not you, holds the truth (w22, docs/architecture/domain-model.md). Scenario: a marketplace takes about 40,000 card payments a day through one provider; the provider posts an event for every status change (received, processing, succeeded, failed, refunded), redelivers any event that does not get a 2xx for up to 3 days, and promises no ordering; roughly 1 event in 200 arrives more than an hour late or never; the provider also offers a 'list payments updated since T' API; finance closes the books at 02:00. Write your design before you look: how the endpoint decides an event really comes from the provider and is well formed, how a redelivered event is recognised, which local status changes are legal and where that rule lives, what the handler does with an event older than the state you already hold and how it could even tell, what it answers for an event about a payment it cannot find, what it stores about every event, and how a periodic sweep against the provider catches what webhooks missed. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Authenticate and validate before trusting anything: verify the provider's signature over the raw body (with a timestamp tolerance against replays) and parse the payload with a schema. Here the route parses any JSON and hands it straight to the processor with no signature check at all, so anyone who knows a provider payment id could post a status.

[w2] Recognise a redelivery by the provider's event id: keep one row per event id under a unique constraint, and answer an already-processed id with success and no further work, so a retried event moves nothing twice.
keyPoints.quote: Inbound processing is idempotent on `providerEventId`, not just on payment id

keyPoints.text: [w3] Keep the legal moves in one table that every writer goes through: PENDING may become SUCCEEDED or FAILED, SUCCEEDED may become REFUNDED, FAILED and REFUNDED have no exits, and asking for the status the payment already has is allowed as a no-op.

[w3] Plan for events that arrive out of order: provider 'received' and 'processing' both map to local PENDING, so a late 'processing' for a payment that already SUCCEEDED asks for a backward move; the handler runs the transition check, which refuses the move with an error response, and the provider then redelivers that stale event for days. Rank the statuses and acknowledge an event that would move backwards with a 2xx, recorded as ignored.

[w2] Know what you can judge ordering by: the payload carries an event id, the provider payment id, a status and an event type, but no provider timestamp or sequence number. Without one, 'older' can only mean lower in the status ranking; ask for the provider's event time or object version and store the last one applied per payment.

[w2] An event for a payment you cannot find is answered with a 404 and nothing is stored, so the provider keeps retrying and your side keeps no trace. Such events are normal (the event can beat your own create commit), so store them as unmatched with a 2xx and match them when the payment appears or when the sweep runs.

[w3] Webhooks are the fast path; what guarantees the end state is a periodic sweep: pull the provider's payments changed since the last run, translate every provider status into its local equivalent and check it against the stored payment. This codebase already does the checking (a mismatch, or a provider-terminal payment with no queued delivery, is written up as an issue) but stops at writing issues; the sweep should push the provider's outcome through the same transition table.

[w2] Store every received event with its payload, received time, processing status, processed time and error, indexed by (processing status, received time), so on-call can list the events that were refused or never matched instead of reading logs.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same consumer in production for a quarter: the provider redelivers an event after the nightly sweep already moved that payment; an event arrives for a payment your database has never seen; a 'processing' event turns up two days after 'succeeded'; a payment you recorded as FAILED is later captured by the provider; and your sweep's view of the provider turns out to come from your own tables. What breaks, how would you notice, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A redelivery after the sweep already applied the same outcome must be harmless, and the event id cannot help, because the sweep's write carried no event id. What saves you is idempotence by state: asking for the status the payment already holds returns without a transition, so the late event is acknowledged and changes nothing. A sweep that wrote the status directly, bypassing the table, would lose that guarantee.

[w3] The two-days-late 'processing' event is refused with an error on every attempt, so the provider retries it for its whole retry window and its dashboard shows your endpoint failing although nothing is wrong with the payment. You notice through the rising non-2xx rate; the repair is the rank check that answers a backward event with success.

[w3] A sweep compared against your own copy of the provider is no safety net: the provider mirror here is a simulated table, and the webhook handler itself overwrites it with each event's status before the transition check. A missed webhook leaves both your copy and your payment stale and in agreement. The sweep must read the provider's API.
keyPoints.quote: This is the simulated external source of truth that reconciliation compares against.

keyPoints.text: [w3] FAILED has no exits, so neither a webhook nor the sweep may record the late capture: the customer was charged and the order is cancelled, and the only signal is a mismatch issue nobody is forced to act on. Repair: an explicit, recorded operator transition (or a refund of the capture), never a silent override of the table.

[w2] The unknown-payment event is lost on your side today; once events are parked as unmatched, the sweep's other direction closes the loop: a provider payment with no local row is already reported as its own issue type, so match parked events against those rows and alert on any still unmatched after a few hours.

[w2] Measure which path is doing the work: each run already stores an issue count in its summary; also track how many payments the sweep had to correct and how stale they were. A growing share fixed by the sweep instead of by webhooks is the early sign that delivery is failing.

[w1] At 40,000 payments a day the sweep cannot reload history: the reconciliation query loads every payment with all of its webhook deliveries on every run. Sweep a window driven by the provider's 'updated since' cursor and page through it.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your webhook-consumer design against the alternatives: webhooks only, polling only, or both; applying the status in the event versus treating the event as a hint and re-reading the payment from the provider; processing inside the HTTP request versus storing the event, answering at once and applying it in a worker; answering a stale event with an error versus acknowledging and ignoring it; event-id deduplication versus idempotence by state; and a sweep that applies corrections versus one that only flags them. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Both, each with a job: webhooks arrive within seconds yet promise neither delivery nor order; a sweep against the provider sees everything but runs late and spends API calls. The design deliberately tolerates a window in which the local record trails the provider, since either path can close it, trading a short inconsistency for a guaranteed final state.
keyPoints.quote: Local status is intentionally allowed to drift behind provider truth until `src/services/webhookService.ts` or `src/services/reconciliationService.ts` corrects it.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Applying the status straight from the payload is cheap but trusts the event's content and its order; treating the event as a hint and fetching the payment's current state from the provider makes order irrelevant (you always apply the latest) and makes a forged body harmless, at the cost of one provider call per event and exposure to its rate limits.

[w2] Processing inside the request (as here, with the whole apply running before the 202) gives an immediate outcome but a slow database turns into provider timeouts and retries; storing the raw event and answering at once makes the acknowledgement fast and durable, at the cost of a worker, a queue to watch and a little more lag.

[w2] An error for a stale event asks the provider to retry something that can never apply; acknowledging and recording it as ignored ends the retries, but needs a view of ignored events so a real bug is not swallowed silently.

[w2] Keep both kinds of idempotence: the unique event-id row proves an event was seen and gives on-call a trail, while comparing against the current status makes a repeated outcome harmless whichever path delivers it, the sweep included.

[w2] Flagging versus correcting: a sweep that never writes a payment status buys safety at the cost of speed, since the provider's outcome waits in an issue queue for a human; the sweep here records issues and one flag event per payment, nothing more. Correct automatically whatever the transition table allows, and queue for people only the moves out of a terminal state.

[w1] A signature check costs secret rotation, clock-skew tolerance and access to the raw body: the route parses the body as JSON first, and the signature must be computed over the exact bytes received. An IP allow-list is simpler but breaks whenever the provider changes its ranges.
